sections.heading: Peasant movements — from breakout to organisation

rows: Planters' forced cultivation; *Nil Darpan* (Dinabandhu Mitra); Indigo Commission — the first press-backed peasant victory
Zamindari rent enhancements; Bengal Tenancy Act 1885
Moneylender bonds burnt; Agriculturists' Relief Act 1879
Tinkathia ended; revenue relief; Bardoli's 30% hike rolled back — Gandhian model satyagrahas
Tenancy + Khilafat ferment turned violent-communal — the cautionary chapter
**Lucknow, 1936 — Swami Sahajanand Saraswati** president; N.G. Ranga general secretary
Class-programme (zamindari abolition, debt relief) inside the national movement

**N.G. Ranga's ryot movement** (Nidubrolu 1923 Ryot Association; India's first **peasant institute, Nidubrolu 1933**); Venkatagiri & Kalipatnam zamindari anti-rent struggles; **Munagala paraganas** struggle
Andhra = the Kisan movement's intellectual home — Ranga its all-India face; fed the 1948 Estates Abolition

Two-thirds share demand; the communist-led **Telangana armed struggle** against Nizam-deshmukh exactions (vetti, illegal levies) — 3,000 villages' communes, land seized, suppressed post-Police Action — the era's most radical agrarian rising, on Telugu soil

items: **Tribal (forest-rights core)**: Santhal Hul (1855-56, Sidhu-Kanhu); **Birsa Munda's Ulgulan (1899-1900** — Munda Raj; CNT Act 1908's germ); Bastar (1910), Tana Bhagat (1914); **Andhra's fituris**: **Rampa 1879**, and **Alluri Sitarama Raju's Manyam rebellion (1922-24)** — podu restrictions, forced labour (vetti), Gudem-Chintapalli police-station raids; betrayed-captured, executed **7 May 1924** — 'Manyam Veerudu' (full treatment HCOA-065); pattern: forest laws + moneylender + missionary/state intrusion → millenarian leadership → ferocious suppression → protective statutes (agency regulations, 1/70's ancestry).

**Workers**: first factory acts (1881/1891); **Madras Labour Union 1918 (B.P. Wadia — India's first modern union)**; **AITUC 1920 (Lala Lajpat Rai first president)**; Trade Union Act 1926; Bombay textile general strikes (1928-29); **Meerut Conspiracy (1929-33)**; split streams (red-flag CPI vs Congress-INTUC 1947 lineage); workers' actions dovetailed with 1930/1942 and the **1946 RIN-solidarity strikes**.

**Women**: from reform's objects to movement's agents — Swadeshi's participation; **WIA (1917, Adyar — Besant, Margaret Cousins)**; **AIWC 1927 (Margaret Cousins; first session Poona)**; franchise campaigns (Madras first to enfranchise women, 1921 — an Andhra-relevant first); Dharasana-Dandi pickets (Sarojini, Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay — who also made Congress socialism feminist); 1942's commanders (Aruna, Usha, Matangini); **Andhra's own — Duvvuri Subbamma, Ponaka Kanakamma, Durgabai Deshmukh (Andhra Mahila Sabha 1937)**; legislative harvest: Sarda Act 1929 → the Hindu Code's post-independence completion.

**Synthesis**: these streams gave nationalism its **social depth** — and their unmet demands (land, forest, wage, gender) became independent India's reform agenda: the 'unfinished business' framing that closes any such answer.

sections.heading: Local and regional movements — the syllabus's second half

items: **Princely-state praja mandals**: All India States' Peoples' Conference (**1927**; Nehru president 1939) — struggles in Rajkot, Mysore, Travancore (temple-entry proclamation 1936), and the **Hyderabad State Congress (1938** — banned at birth; Vande Mataram movement in Nizam's colleges; the join-India struggle 1947-48) — directly the Telangana-Andhra context.

**Linguistic-identity movements as nationalism's dialect**: the **Andhra movement** (from 1913 Bapatla — HCOA-064's full story) modelled how regional identity and Indian nationalism reinforced; parallels — Utkal (Orissa 1936 as reward), Kannada unification, Kerala's Aikya Kerala.

**Issue movements**: temple-entry (Vaikom 1924-25, Guruvayur 1931-32 — K. Kelappan; Andhra's own 1929-39 campaigns), anti-untouchability under Gandhi's Harijan Sevak Sangh (1932), prohibition-picketing, students' (AISF 1936) and princely-women's fronts — the capillaries of the national body.

**Reading**: the freedom struggle was a **coalition of struggles** — class, caste, region, language, princely-subject — the Congress umbrella channelled (and sometimes deferred) them; independent India's federal-social architecture (linguistic states, reservations, land reform) is their settlement.

sections.heading: Unity and its unmaking — the double helix

blocks.text: Modern India carried **two intertwined strands**: composite nationalism (1857's joint proclamations under Bahadur Shah; Hindu-Muslim Swadeshi platforms; **Lucknow Pact 1916**; the **Khilafat-Non-Cooperation fusion (1920-22)** — communal unity's noon) and **communalism** — the ideology that religious communities have antagonistic secular interests. Communalism was **modern, not medieval**: a product of colonial sociology (census categories, communal electorates 1909), elite competition for jobs-seats, revivalist idioms on both sides (shuddhi-sangathan vs tabligh-tanzim, 1920s), and the Raj's balancing strategy — 'divide et impera' as constitutional design.

rows: Antagonistic; separate nationhood — fear and hate politics
Savarkar's two-nations (1937 Ahmedabad address), **Lahore 1940**; Direct Action 1946

blocks.text: **Milestone chain**: 1909 electorates → 1916 legitimation → 1920-22 unity peak → **1920s riot decade** (Moplah 1921, Kohat 1924; Gandhi's 21-day unity fast 1924) → Nehru Report vs 14 Points (1928-29) → Communal Award 1932 → **1937 office rejection** (League's grievance manufacturing: Pirpur report) → Lahore 1940 → Cripps' opt-out 1942 → **Direct Action 16 Aug 1946 → Noakhali-Bihar** (Gandhi's finest walking hour) → Partition's ~10-15 lakh dead, ~1.5 crore displaced.

sections.heading: The unity tradition — and the Andhra register

items: **The unity actors**: Gandhi (unity as creed — 1924 fast, Noakhali barefoot, the last fast for Delhi's Muslims, Jan 1948); **Maulana Azad** (*composite nationalism* theorised — Ghubar-e-Khatir; Congress president 1940-46 warning against Partition's costs); **Badshah Khan** (nonviolent Pashtun nationalism — 'thrown to the wolves'); the **Deoband ulema's anti-Partition line (Madani's muttahida qaumiyat)**; JP-Lohia's socialist secularism; countless local peace committees of 1946-47.

**Why unity lost (the causes paragraph)**: colonial institutional grooves (electorates) + elite job-seat competition + economic backwardness making religion the mobilising idiom + Congress's failures (mass contact programme's collapse 1937-39; ministries' insensitivities) + League's fear machinery + war's opportunity (Linlithgow needing counterweights) — **multi-causal, never mono-causal**.

**Andhra register**: coastal Andhra largely escaped the riot decade's worst — composite Telugu public culture (Muslim reformers in the Andhra movement; **Sheikh/Dudekula participation in Congress campaigns**); Hyderabad state inverted the frame — **Razakar violence (1947-48)** and the Police Action's aftermath (Sundarlal report's sobering findings) is the region's own communal-tragedy chapter, resolved into the composite politics of post-1956 AP; cite both the escape and the exception.

**Closing frame**: communalism is nationalism's shadow-self — fought then by composite mobilisation, fought now by constitutional secularism (Arts 25-28, S.R. Bommai's secularism-as-basic-structure) — history's lesson standing guard in law.

sections.heading: 🏺 Deep mastery — communalism, unity & Partition

items: **The double helix of unity & division:** the parallel growth of nationalism and communalism — **separate electorates (1909), Lucknow Pact (1916), Khilafat unity (1920), then the Nehru Report rupture, the two-nation theory, and the 1940 Lahore (Pakistan) Resolution**.

**Roots of communalism:** colonial 'divide and rule', uneven socio-economic development among communities, the politicisation of religious identity, and elite competition — not primordial hatred (the 'constructed' view).
**The unity tradition:** the composite-culture ideal, Gandhi's Hindu-Muslim unity, and the secular-nationalist mainstream that Partition tragically could not fully hold.
**Andhra register:** the region's relatively composite social fabric and the way linguistic identity (Telugu) cut across religious lines in the province's politics.
